description:
We are a multidisciplinary squad of four engineers operating at the intersection of Data Science, Artificial Intelligence, and Cybersecurity. Our background covers intelligent systems, advanced analytics, predictive modeling, and resilient digital infrastructure.

Our Mission: Space-grade solutions shouldn't just be smart—they must be reliable, interpretable, and secure by design. We combine AI with strict data integrity to build end-to-end solutions for real NASA challenges.
summary:
**Crew Health Compass**, developed by team **fourNPC's**, is an offline-first, personalized astronaut health-monitoring platform designed to support human health awareness during long-duration space missions.

Unlike traditional monitoring approaches that rely on fixed thresholds alone, our solution considers each astronaut's personal baseline and activity context to identify unusual physiological patterns and provide understandable explanations.

Our working prototype combines three complementary features:

1. **Personalized Health Monitor:** An interactive astronaut interface that analyzes manual health check-ins using statistical anomaly detection and synthetic mission histories.
2. **NASA Biological Passport:** A research dashboard analyzing 302 biomarkers from NASA's OSD-575 dataset, comparing postflight measurements with individual preflight baselines and visualizing biological changes over time.
3. **Mission Environment:** An interactive explorer of 5,971 real NASA Curiosity RAD radiation measurements, highlighting historical changes in the Martian radiation environment.

Built with Python, FastAPI, React, and local analytics, Crew Health Compass operates without continuous internet connectivity.

By transforming complex physiological, biological, and environmental data into accessible, explainable insights, our project explores how future space missions could support greater astronaut autonomy and more informed health monitoring.
details:
Crew Health Compass — Project Details

1. Project Overview

Crew Health Compass, developed by team fourNPC's, is an offline-first astronaut health-monitoring and research platform designed to make complex space-health information more personalized, understandable, and accessible.

Our project addresses a fundamental challenge of long-duration space exploration: How can astronauts recognize meaningful changes in their health when immediate medical support and reliable communication with Earth may be limited?

Rather than simply displaying physiological measurements, Crew Health Compass combines personal baselines, context-aware statistical analysis, real NASA research datasets, and interactive visualizations to help users explore and understand health-related changes.

2. How Our Solution Works

The platform consists of three complementary modules:

A. Personalized Health Monitor

Astronauts can manually enter physiological measurements, including heart rate, respiratory rate, blood pressure, sleep duration, and mood, alongside their current activity context.

Our analytical engine compares supported measurements against the astronaut's historical baseline using robust statistical methods, including median and Median Absolute Deviation (MAD).

Instead of relying exclusively on universal thresholds, the system considers individual variation and measurement context.

The results are displayed through an interactive astronaut visualization, highlighting affected physiological systems and providing evidence-based explanations.

We also developed an experimental local machine-learning component using Isolation Forest. It was evaluated on held-out synthetic mission data but remains disabled for ordinary manual monitoring because it has not been validated on real manual inputs.

B. NASA Biological Passport

Using real NASA OSD-575 research data, we developed an interactive biological analysis system covering 302 biomarkers across four measurement panels.

The platform calculates individual preflight baselines, compares postflight measurements, and visualizes longitudinal biological trajectories.

Users can explore measurements for four coded study participants, compare biomarker changes, and examine automatically generated evidence summaries.

The system distinguishes measured changes, available laboratory reference intervals, and insufficient data without presenting exploratory research findings as medical diagnoses.

C. Mission Environment — Mars Radiation History

We integrated 5,971 historical radiation measurements from NASA's Curiosity rover Radiation Assessment Detector (RAD).

This module provides an interactive timeline of the Martian radiation environment and highlights the documented May 20, 2024 solar radiation event.

Users can explore historical dose-rate measurements, examine changes over time, and understand environmental conditions relevant to future human exploration.

These environmental measurements are presented separately from personal astronaut health assessments.

3. Technologies and Development Tools

Our prototype was developed using:

  • Python: Data processing, statistical analysis, biomarker comparisons, and experimental machine learning.
  • FastAPI: Backend services connecting the analytics engine to the user interface.
  • React and JavaScript: Interactive frontend dashboards and astronaut health visualizations.
  • Scikit-learn: Experimental Isolation Forest anomaly detection.
  • NASA Open Science Data: Real biological and Martian environmental measurements.
  • Synthetic Mission Datasets: Context-aware monitoring development and controlled evaluation.
  • Git and GitHub: Collaborative development, version control, and integration.

The application is designed to operate locally without depending on continuous internet connectivity or external AI inference services. No specialized hardware is required for the current software prototype.

4. Innovation and Creativity

Our innovation lies in combining three complementary perspectives into one platform:

Personalized monitoring: Interpreting physiological measurements relative to an astronaut's own historical patterns and activity context.

Biological exploration: Transforming complex NASA laboratory research data into accessible personal baseline comparisons and longitudinal visualizations.

Environmental awareness: Connecting astronaut-health research with historical measurements of the Martian radiation environment.

We also prioritized explainability. Rather than providing an unexplained anomaly score, the system presents supporting measurements, baseline information, and data limitations.

The interactive astronaut interface makes statistical findings more intuitive, while the Biological Passport and radiation explorer allow users to investigate authentic NASA research evidence.

5. Design Considerations and Limitations

During development, our team considered several important factors:

  • Offline operation: Supporting mission scenarios with limited connectivity.
  • Personalization: Accounting for individual physiological differences.
  • Activity context: Avoiding inappropriate comparisons between different measurement conditions.
  • Transparency: Showing why a measurement is considered unusual.
  • Scientific integrity: Clearly separating real NASA measurements from synthetic monitoring data.
  • Data limitations: Explicitly handling missing observations, unavailable reference intervals, and insufficient historical baselines.
  • Safety: Avoiding unsupported medical diagnoses, treatment recommendations, or personal radiation-risk predictions.

Our current prototype is a research and technology demonstration, not a clinically validated medical device.

6. Intended Impact and Future Development

Crew Health Compass explores how future astronaut health-monitoring systems could provide more personalized and understandable information while reducing dependence on continuous communication with Earth.

Its potential benefits include improved awareness of physiological changes, more accessible scientific evidence, and better support for autonomous health-monitoring workflows.

Future development would focus on validating the system with representative astronaut physiological datasets, collaborating with medical experts to establish approved monitoring protocols, improving sensor integration, and evaluating performance under realistic mission conditions.

Our vision is to help make future space exploration not only more ambitious, but also more human-centered — by turning complex space-health data into understandable evidence that supports astronaut autonomy.
